Chapter 24

Motion with intent

What moves in Meridian and what is not allowed to: the design brief’s two lists as the rules, four mechanisms and when each is the right one, the one custom transition with css(t, u), three Svelte transitions and one animate:flip, a Tween for the tab bar, CSS keyframes that Bits UI waits for, a phone menu whose motion ends outside the accessibility tree, the svelte/easing table — and every built-in the project leaves out, with the rule that keeps it out.

By the end of this chapter

Choose between a CSS animation, a Svelte transition, an animation and a motion value for a given movement; write a custom transition; honour reduced motion in each; and say no to the motion a design does not need.

The design system set the budget; this chapter spends it, and the rules for spending it are not taste. The design brief has two lists. “What animates, exactly” is a table, and it is exhaustive: every movement in the product is a row, with its duration token, its curve and the file it lives in — a dialog rises 8px, a bottom sheet slides on the iOS curve, the tab indicator translates, a new stop gets a highlight that fades, the live dot pulses because the pulse is information. “What never animates” is the other list: text colour, layout (no height, width or margin transitions anywhere), the header’s border, table sorting, presence chips, numbers, anything parallax, and anything at all under reduced motion. A movement that is not in the first list is not built, and a movement in the second is refused even when a library makes it one word. That is what “with intent” means here: motion that explains a change of state — where the dialog came from, which tab you are on now, which card just arrived — and nothing that decorates.

There are four ways to move something in a Svelte app, and each has its own job. CSS — a transition or @keyframes — for anything that stays in the document and changes state: hover, press, open, closed. It reads the --dur-* tokens, so reduced motion reaches it for free. A Svelte transition (transition:, in:, out:) for an element that enters or leaves the document because of state — the one thing CSS cannot do on its own, because once an element is removed there is nothing left to animate. An animation (animate:) for an item that moves to a new place in a keyed list. And a motion value — Tween or Spring from svelte/motion — for a number that has to glide to its new value while a script reads it every frame. The hero’s GSAP timeline is the fifth, used once, and chapter 23 says why.

CSS first, and a library that waits for it

The dialogs are the largest movement in the product, and they have no JavaScript animation at all. Bits UI renders data-state="open" while a dialog is up and flips it to closed just before unmounting — and, the comment says, waits for any CSS animation on the element to finish first. So the enter and the exit are two keyframe rules each: the scrim fades, the phone’s sheet slides up on --ease-sheet and down on --ease-in, and from 40em the panel scales from 0.96 and rises 8px. The exit is shorter than the entrance on purpose (--dur-3 against --dur-4): a person who has decided to close something wants it gone. Under reduced motion every token is 0ms, the animation ends the moment it starts, and the dialog simply appears and disappears.

That is the line between CSS and a Svelte transition. CSS can animate an element’s *leaving* only when something keeps the element in the document until the animation ends — Bits UI does it for its own components by waiting. For an element of yours inside an {#if}, Svelte is the thing that waits: the documentation’s rule is that when a block is transitioning out, “all elements inside it, including those that do not have their own transitions, are kept in the DOM until every transition in the block has been completed”. An element that never leaves — the update banner, which reloads the page instead of closing, the header’s sheet, the tab indicator — needs no transition at all, and gets CSS.

The update banner is the plainest case: one keyframe rule, arrive, from 16px lower and transparent, on --dur-4 with --ease-out, played once when the banner is rendered. It has no exit because it has no way to leave — the button reloads the page — and an in:fly would have done the same thing with a JavaScript import and a reduced-motion check of its own.

One custom transition

A transition is a function of three arguments — the element, the parameters written in the directive, and an options object, whose options.direction says which way this run goes ('in', 'out' or 'both') — that returns a TransitionConfig: delay, duration, easing, and one of css or tick. css(t, u) returns a string of CSS for a moment of the transition: t runs from 0 to 1 on the way in and from 1 back to 0 on the way out, so 1 is always the element as it naturally is, and u is 1 - t. Easing is applied before css sees t, so pop writes a straight line — opacity t, scale from 0.6 to 1 — and cubicOut bends it. Svelte calls css many times *before* the transition starts and turns the answers into keyframes for a Web Animation, which a browser can run off the main thread; tick(t, u) is called on every frame instead, for the rare movement that CSS cannot describe (the documentation’s example types a sentence out letter by letter). The rule is theirs: “If it’s possible to use css instead of tick, do so.”

Two more forms exist and pop needs neither. The third argument, options, carries direction — in, out or both — for a transition that should move differently on the way out. And a transition may return a *function* that returns the config instead of the config itself; that function is called in the next microtask, after every transition starting in the same update has been created, which is how crossfade lets a leaving element and an arriving one find each other before either decides how to move.

Why pop asks about reduced motion itself

Because nothing else will. The tokens in tokens.css reach CSS animations, and the documentation says plainly that Svelte’s transitions are not those: they “are driven by the Web Animations API rather than by CSS. A global @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) rule that zeroes transition-duration and animation-duration therefore has no effect on them.” So every transition in the project reads reducedMotion — prefersReducedMotion from svelte/motion, under the app’s name (chapter 23) — and takes a duration of 0 when it is set — pop in its own body, so a component that uses it never has to remember, and the built-ins at the place they are used.

in: is a transition that plays only on the way in. The check mark that replaces a copy icon pops in, and the copy icon it replaced simply goes: an out: on it would hold both icons in the button for 160ms, side by side, and the button would grow and shrink — layout, which never animates. The invite link’s block fades in rather than sliding open for the same reason. Both are *local*, which is the default in Svelte 5: “Local transitions only play when the block they belong to is created or destroyed, not when parent blocks are created or destroyed.” The fade belongs to {#if inviteUrl}, so it plays at the one moment it explains — the link has just been made — and never because something around it appeared. |global is the opt-in for the other behaviour, and a screen built from global transitions animates every piece of itself at once whenever a page or a tab first renders; the project has none.

transition: is the bidirectional kind: the same function on the way in and on the way out, and “it can be smoothly reversed while the transition is in progress” — toggle the locate button twice quickly and the pill turns round where it is rather than finishing and starting again. It is the one Svelte transition on the map, on the one element that comes and goes there: “Finding you…” while the browser looks, “Location is not available.” if it cannot. role="status" makes a screen reader say it; the fade is for everybody else.

One animation, in the one list that reorders

animate: is for a different event from a transition: an item that stays in a keyed {#each} but moves to another index. The documentation’s three conditions are the whole contract — it runs “when the contents of a keyed each block are re-ordered”, it does not run “when an element is added or removed”, and the directive must sit on an *immediate* child of the keyed block, which is why it is on the <li> and not on the card inside it. flip measures where the element was (First) and where it is now (Last), moves it back to the first place with a transform (Invert), and lets it go (Play). svelte-dnd-action does its own FLIP for the card being dragged, and flipDurationMs tells it how long Svelte’s will take for the others, so both read one duration — 240ms, or 0 under reduced motion. There are no in: or out: on the items: the library says it does not work with them, and a stop that arrives gets the brief’s “highlight, not a bounce” instead, the fresh mark the effect sets for 1.2 seconds.

A custom animation has the same shape as a custom transition, with one difference in its arguments: (node, { from, to }, params), where from and to are the element’s DOMRect before and after the reorder, returning an AnimationConfig — delay, duration, easing, css, tick. The project writes none, because flip is the reorder the brief asks for, and the only list that reorders by hand is the itinerary. The expenses table re-sorts in place, with no movement at all: the brief lists table sorting among the things that never animate.

A value that moves: Tween, and the Spring beside it

The tab indicator is one 2px bar that slides between tabs, and its position is a Tween: new Tween(initial, { duration, easing }), then set(target) — which returns a promise for when it arrives — and .current, which the markup reads on every frame and hands to the stylesheet as style:--x and style:--w (chapter 23). The options given to set override the defaults for that one move, and { duration: 0 } is how a tween jumps: the first placement, a resize, and every move under reduced motion. Tween.of(() => value) is the other constructor, a tween bound to whatever the function returns, created during component initialisation — and the project does not use it, because the obvious place for it is the trip header’s total distance, and the brief says numbers never count up.

Spring is the tween’s physical sibling, available since Svelte 5.8: instead of a duration it has stiffness, damping and precision, and a value set while it is moving keeps its momentum. Its set takes { instant: true } to jump — where a Tween takes { duration: 0 } — and preserveMomentum in milliseconds for a fling, and Spring.of binds it to a function as Tween.of does. The place it belongs is the waypoint library’s compass needle, swinging to a new bearing (chapter 08); it is not there because the library promises svelte ^5.0.0 to anybody who installs it, and a class from 5.8 would break that promise. Both replace the stores tweened and spring, which Svelte 5 still exports and marks deprecated: they did the same job behind subscribe and $value.

A menu whose motion ends outside the accessibility tree

The phone’s menu sheet looks like a textbook slide, and the brief chose otherwise for three reasons. The sheet is always in the document, because the menu button’s aria-controls must point at something, and a transition only plays when an {#if} adds or removes an element. And slide animates height, padding and margin — layout, which never animates. (It also measures the element it moves, and Svelte warns at run time, as transition_slide_display, when the element’s display is contents, inline or table, where that measuring cannot work.) So the sheet is revealed by a clip-path from the top — a mask, not a box changing size — and its links fade in 30ms apart through --i, the custom property each link is given in the markup.

The part that matters more than the look is the last line of the closed state: visibility: hidden, after a delay as long as the clip takes. A clipped element is invisible to the eye and perfectly visible to a screen reader and to the Tab key — a closed menu that a keyboard can still walk into. visibility: hidden takes the links out of the accessibility tree and out of the tab order, and the delay lets the clip finish before it does. Opening switches visibility at once and runs the clip; closing runs the clip and then switches. The test proves the result rather than the CSS:

On the Pixel 7 profile only, because a desktop has no menu. Before the menu opens, a query by role cannot find the Explore link at all — Playwright’s role queries see what the accessibility tree sees — so toBeHidden() passes on an element that is not there for a screen reader either. Opened, it is visible; Escape closes it, the button says aria-expanded="false", focus is back on it, and the link is gone from the tree again. Delete visibility: hidden from the closed sheet and the first assertion fails, with the sheet still perfectly clipped on screen.

The easing table

svelte/easing exports thirty-one functions: linear, and ten families in three forms each — in, out and inOut, as in cubicIn, cubicOut, cubicInOut. The form says where the movement is fast. …Out starts fast and settles — the curve for something *arriving*, and cubicOut is the nearest built-in to the --ease-out token, which a JavaScript easing cannot read. …In starts slowly and leaves fast — for something going away, the role --ease-in plays in CSS, “exits only”. …InOut is slow at both ends, for something moving from one place on screen to another, like --ease-inout. The family says how strongly:

  • sine, quad — the gentlest. A fade that should barely be noticed.
  • cubic — the project’s default: cubicOut for the tab indicator and for pop.
  • quart, quint, expo — the same shape, steeper each time: most of the movement in the first moment, then a long settle. GSAP’s power3.out on the hero is the quart curve under another name.
  • circ — a quarter circle: abrupt at one end, very soft at the other.
  • back, elastic, bounce — they overshoot the target and come back, or bounce off it. Declined everywhere: an overshoot is a bounce, and the brief’s word for a new stop is “a highlight, not a bounce”.
  • linear — no easing: for progress and for anything continuous. Nothing here needs it; the live dot’s pulse is CSS.

What is left out, and the rule that does it

  • fade|global or in:scale out:fade on presence chips — “Presence chips entering/leaving — they appear.” A person arriving with a bounce is a slot machine. (in: and out: together are the non-bidirectional pair: a different movement each way, and no reversing halfway.)
  • Tween.of on the total distance — “Numbers (totals, distances) — no count-up.”
  • fly on the update banner — the CSS arrive above does it, with no exit to need a transition.
  • slide on the menu sheet — above: the sheet never leaves the document, and slide animates layout.
  • draw on a trip card’s route — draw traces an SVG path’s stroke over time, and it is not in the brief’s table: card hover is the only card motion.
  • crossfade when a stop moves to another day — crossfade({ fallback }) returns a pair, [send, receive], and an element sent with a key flies to the element received with the same key. It needs out: and in: on the items, and items in a dndzone may not have them; the brief says list reorder is FLIP only.
  • scale and blur — scale grows a thing from a point, which is a bounce by another name; blur makes the text being read unreadable mid-movement, and the brief will not move the text you are reading.
  • unmount(component, { outro: true }) — plays a component’s outros before it leaves, and its promise resolves when they have finished; mount plays intros unless intro: false is passed. Both are for a component mounted by hand, and this project mounts none — even the custom element is mounted by the browser.
  • Skeleton loaders — “Skeletons — None.” Every await resolves on the server; a shimmer would invent latency to show off.

Why reduced motion means none, not less

Because “less” is a judgement made on somebody else’s behalf, and the setting exists for people for whom motion is not a matter of taste — vestibular disorders, migraine, attention. So in this project the setting turns every duration to 0, turns view transitions off (the root layout starts none, chapter 25), stops the globe’s flight and its camera, makes the map jump instead of fly, sets flip to 0, and never attaches the hero timeline at all. The live dot is the only thing that pulses, and under reduced motion it holds still too. Every one of those checks reads the same query, and the visual suite runs with reduced motion on, so a screen that only settles correctly with motion would fail there (chapter 46).

Checkpoint

  • Given a movement, you can say whether it is CSS, a transition, an animation or a motion value, and why.
  • You can write a custom transition with css(t, u), say what t and u are on the way in and out, and say when tick is the right answer.
  • You can say what local means for a transition, and what |global would change.
  • You know the three conditions under which animate: runs, and why the itinerary’s items have no in: or out:.
  • You can say why the phone menu ends on visibility: hidden, and what the end-to-end test proves.
  • You can name the rule in the brief that keeps each left-out built-in out.
